questions.short_title: NRB + nasal cannula inferior to flush-rate preoxygenation
questions.question: How did combined NRB plus nasal cannula preoxygenation (25 L/min each) compare with flush-rate NRB?
options: It was inferior to flush rate
It matched flush rate at 15 L/min
It was equivalent to flush rate
It outperformed flush rate
questions.explanation: Expired oxygen reached 75% versus 85% with flush-rate NRB, a difference that failed the non-inferiority margin. The findings come from healthy volunteers, so real emergency patients may differ.

questions.short_title: Post-OHCA outcomes at Victorian Heart Hospital
questions.question: A colleague says the 50.4% survival to discharge at the dedicated cardiac hospital proves post-arrest patients do better there than under usual state-wide pathways. What's the best response?
options: The survival figure matches national averages, so triage practices can stay unchanged
The cohort was small and highly selected, so the figure isn't comparable to population-based OHCA outcomes
Survival dropped sharply because a quarter of patients needed interhospital transfer for cardiac causes
The benefit only applies to patients with non-shockable rhythms
questions.explanation: The high survival came from a small, single tertiary cohort with favourable features like 92.6% prehospital ROSC and mostly shockable rhythms. The authors specifically warn against reading it as superiority over population-based outcomes, and transfers were mostly for non-cardiac causes.

questions.question: Among US children not transported after a paediatric 9-1-1 call, what proportion had a repeat call with transport to ED within 72 hours?
options: About 40%
About 11%
About 16%
About 1%
questions.explanation: Only 1% of non-transported children were re-called and transported within 72 hours, and hospitalisation or death at re-call was rare. The data are retrospective US records with only one third hospital-linked, so they don't directly reflect Australian practice.

questions.short_title: Stroke care gaps for First Nations patients
questions.question: According to the linked-data study of EMS-attended stroke and TIA patients, where was the main disparity in care for First Nations patients?
options: Adjusted 30- and 90-day mortality was clearly higher
They were less likely to be transported to hospital at all
Paramedics were less likely to perform a stroke assessment
Stroke or TIA was less often identified at the emergency call
questions.explanation: Call-taker identification rates were comparable, but First Nations patients received a paramedic stroke assessment less often (58.2% vs 67.3%) and were taken less often to thrombectomy-capable hospitals. Adjusted mortality was actually similar, and the Victorian data with only 287 First Nations patients limit precision and generalisability.

questions.short_title: What OHCA care is worth paying for
questions.question: According to this systematic review of economic evaluations, which prehospital OHCA strategy was found to be more cost-effective than its alternative?
options: Delivering ECPR in the prehospital setting rather than waiting until arrival in hospital
Early defibrillation rather than EMT-delivered ALS
Paramedic-led ALS rather than emergency physician-led ALS
Transporting every arrest patient rather than applying termination-of-resuscitation rules
questions.explanation: Prehospital ECPR came out more cost-effective than in-hospital ECPR strategies, with ICERs of AU$27,323 to $44,000 per QALY. Keep in mind the studies spanned different health systems and funding models, so the results don't transfer neatly to any one context.

questions.short_title: Nearly half of paediatric doses off-protocol
questions.question: What pattern of off-protocol paediatric drug dosing did the registry study find?
options: Mostly underdoses, worst with ondansetron and intranasal doses
Mostly overdoses driven by weight estimation error
Evenly split over and underdoses across all routes
Mostly underdoses confined to intramuscular fentanyl
questions.explanation: Of the 46.4% of doses deviating at least 20% from protocol, 79.9% were underdoses, with ondansetron and the intranasal route the biggest drivers. Weight estimation error showed no association, and registry flags may capture deliberate titration within permitted ranges.

questions.question: A colleague cites the Canadian methoxyflurane feasibility study as proof the drug causes large pain reductions in trauma patients. What is the main problem with that claim?
options: Protocol compliance was too low for the results to be reliable
Pain scores were only documented in about half of treated patients
The study had no comparator arm, so the improvement can't be attributed to methoxyflurane alone
Most patients had severe side effects that inflated their reported pain scores
questions.explanation: It was a single-arm feasibility study with no control group, so natural pain course or other care could explain the fall from 8/10 to 5/10. Compliance was actually high at 95%, side effects were mostly mild, and pain scores were documented in 90% of treated patients.

questions.short_title: Two-thirds of stroke patients delay seeking care
questions.question: In the pooled analysis of prehospital delay before ischaemic stroke care, roughly what proportion of patients delayed seeking help?
options: About 1 in 4
About 9 in 10
About 1 in 3
About 2 in 3
questions.explanation: The pooled incidence of prehospital delay was 67.7%, so about two-thirds of patients delayed. The evidence was low certainty and dominated by Asian studies with inconsistent definitions of delay, so apply the figure with caution locally.
